title: SNAP work requirements reduced participation without increasing labor supply in a five-state study
source_unit: Census CES Working Paper 26-46 using linked administrative SNAP and employment data from five states
geography: United States; five states, counties and states with phased SNAP work-requirement reinstatement during the 2010s

observations.period: Post-Great-Recession suspension and 2010s county/state reinstatement of SNAP work requirements; paper published July 2026

denominator.unit: linked SNAP-administrative and employment-data policy comparison across five states

participation.value: work requirements reduced SNAP participation by 7%

labor_supply.value: work requirements did not increase labor supply

screening.value: lower-income individuals were disproportionately screened out

policy_purpose.value: the study evaluates work requirements as a screening device

welfare_interpretation.value: the authors' welfare framework finds social costs exceed budget savings

observations.method: The authors use linked administrative SNAP and employment data from five states and a triple-differences design exploiting county and state timing of work-requirement reinstatement.
observations.uncertainty: This is a Census CES working paper and not a Census Bureau endorsement. The estimates cover five states and the studied policy periods; participation loss is not itself a complete measure of food security, employment quality, household adaptation, or long-run welfare.
observations.subgroup: SNAP recipients and eligible adults classified under the able-bodied-adults-without-dependents rules, with distributional differences by income; effects may differ by disability, care, transportation, local labor demand, administrative capacity, and state implementation.
observations.counterinterpretation: Work requirements may interact with reporting, exemption, recertification, employment quality, local labor demand, and administrative churn. A participation decline could reflect procedural loss, changed eligibility, non-use, or exit; the abstract does not identify each pathway or later food security.

related_sources.claim: The official paper provides the five-state linked-data design, triple-differences method, participation and labor-supply estimates, subgroup pattern, and welfare framework.

boundary: This record adds a work-requirement-to-participation pathway. It does not establish a universal effect across SNAP rules, states, periods, or groups, and does not directly measure food security, health, household income, administrative burden, or political response.
